title: Illusion Against Illusion
subtitle: Pradyumna meets Shamvara's magic on the battlefield
story:
Across the field of battle came Shamvara's golden chariot, and the demon king rode it like a storm. "O hero," he told his charioteer, "take my car to the enemy soon. With arrows I will kill him who has done me wrong." He meant the youth who stood on the far side of the field with a bow already strung: Pradyumna, the son of Krishna and Rukmini, the baby Shamvara had once snatched away and meant to destroy, grown now into a man who had already cut down the demon's four chief ministers, one after another, until the army itself had fled from him.

Pradyumna watched the golden car approach and set a golden arrow to his string. His first shaft struck home, cutting to Shamvara's very vitals, and the demon king reeled in his seat, clutching the reins, and lost consciousness. When he came back to himself a few moments later, rage had made him reckless. He snatched up his bow and loosed seventy sharpened arrows at Krishna's son, and Pradyumna met them with seven shafts that cut all seventy into seven parts before they could reach him. Then seventy winged arrows flew back the other way, and then a thousand, until the sky was so thick with shafts that even the sun was hidden. Shamvara dispelled that darkness with his thunderbolt and showered arrows on Pradyumna's car; Pradyumna, light of hand, sliced them into pieces as they came. In the end it was the arrows that gave out first.

Then the demon changed his art entirely. By his illusory powers he showered the field with trees, and Pradyumna, beside himself with anger, burned them all to ash with fiery weapons. Shamvara answered with a downpour of stones, and Pradyumna swept them from the battlefield with weapons of air. Next came the beasts, lions, tigers, bears, monkeys, horses, camels, asses, and elephants like clouds, hurled at his car, and the Gandharva weapons cut the whole illusory herd into pieces. So Shamvara raised the stakes: elephants with sixty heads each, mad for battle, decked for war and ridden by expert drivers. Pradyumna answered illusion with illusion, calling up lions of his own, and the illusory lions destroyed the illusory elephants as the sun sends away the night.

Illusion followed illusion. Shamvara cast the Sunmohini Maya, the fascinating spell that the great architect Maya himself had fashioned, and Pradyumna checked it with his weapon of consciousness. Shamvara sent lions again; Pradyumna sent the sharabhas, eight-legged creatures of claws and teeth, and they pursued the lions as the wind scatters clouds. For the first time the demon king doubted himself. "Alas, how stupid I am," he thought. "Why did I not kill him in his infancy? Now he has attained to youth and mastered every weapon. Only one illusion remains to me, the dread illusion of serpents, which the great god Hara himself instructed me in, and which no one else knows. Let me spread it, and see whether this powerful magician can be consumed."

He spread it. Serpents full of burning venom coiled around Pradyumna, his car, his horses, and his charioteer, and bound them all fast. But Pradyumna thought of the garudas, the eagle-kings who feast on serpents, and at the very thought they came wheeling down and began to destroy the venomous illusion. When the last serpent dissolved, the gods and the asuras watching from the sky cried out together: "Well done! Well done! O mighty-armed son of Rukmini, the illusion is dispelled by you, and we are pleased."

Shamvara stood in his golden car with nothing left of his magic. But there remained one weapon that was not magic at all, a golden club shaped like the rod of Death itself, which the goddess Uma had conferred on him long ago, saying it could dispel all forms of illusion and kill all asuras. He had already sent many demons to the abode of Yama with it. Now, while the applause of the gods still rang over the field, his hand closed on it.
reflection: The duel is a contest of knowledge as much as of strength. Shamvara's every illusion is genuine craft, and each one is met by a counter-craft in the boy he failed to kill, maya answered by maya, illusion by illusion, until nothing the demon knows is unknown to his enemy. What defeats him is not a larger army but a deeper mastery of the same art.
next_story_tease: But Shamvara was reaching for the golden club that no weapon could withstand, and in the sky above the battlefield a figure was already descending to meet him.
hero_scene: Illusory serpents coiling around Pradyumna's chariot, horses and charioteer, while great garudas wheel down from a dark, arrow-thick sky to tear the venomous illusion apart, the gods and asuras watching from above.
